title: The King Burns the Scroll
summary: In the fourth year of King Jehoiakim, God tells Jeremiah to write down every word he has spoken, in the hope that Judah will hear and turn. Baruch writes the scroll at Jeremiah's dictation and reads it aloud in the temple on a fast day, then to the royal officials, and finally it is read to the king. Jehoiakim cuts it apart column by column and burns it in his brazier, and God has Jeremiah dictate the whole scroll again, with more added.
story: Chapters 34 to 39 move toward the fall of Jerusalem, but this chapter steps back about eighteen years to show why the fall came. Jeremiah has been preaching for more than two decades, since the thirteenth year of Josiah (1:2). Now God asks for something new: a written record of it all, so that the whole message can be heard at once. The chapter is the Bible's most detailed account of how a prophet's words became a book, and it is also a portrait of a king's response to the word of God. Jehoiakim's knife and fire answer the question the scroll asks. The rewritten scroll at the end explains, in part, why we have the book of Jeremiah at all.
historical:
The fourth year of Jehoiakim (verse 1) is 605 BC, the year Nebuchadnezzar of Babylon defeated Egypt at Carchemish on the Euphrates (46:2) and became the dominant power in the region. The public reading takes place in the ninth month of the fifth year (verse 9), in the winter of 604 BC. The Babylonian Chronicle, a series of cuneiform tablets recording the main events of each year of the Babylonian kings, reports that in Nebuchadnezzar's first year he marched into the west and destroyed the Philistine city of Ashkelon in the month of Kislev, the ninth month. Many scholars think the fast in Jerusalem was proclaimed in response to that threat on Judah's doorstep, though the chapter doesn't say so.

Several of the officials named here belong to a family we meet elsewhere. Shaphan was the royal scribe who read the rediscovered book of the law to King Josiah (2 Kings 22), and his son Ahikam had protected Jeremiah from execution (26:24). In 1982, excavations in the City of David directed by Yigal Shiloh uncovered a burned building containing dozens of clay seal impressions (bullae), one of which bears the name Gemaryahu son of Shaphan. Most scholars think this is probably the Gemariah of verses 10 to 12, though the identification can't be proven. Clay bullae naming Berekhyahu son of Neriyahu the scribe (Baruch's full name) have also been published, but they came through the antiquities market rather than an excavation, and their authenticity is disputed.
cultural:
A scroll in Judah was made of papyrus or leather, written in columns and rolled up. The Hebrew word translated "columns" in verse 23 literally means doors, a picture of the tall panels of writing on the roll. Papyrus burns quickly and cleanly, which fits the scene, but the text doesn't name the material. The scribe's knife was the small blade scribes used to trim reed pens and cut scrolls. Palaces had rooms designed for the cold months, and in the ninth month (roughly our December) a brazier of coals burned in the king's winter quarters.

Public fasts were called in times of danger, when the people gathered at the temple to confess sin and ask for mercy. That is why Jeremiah chooses a fast day: the crowd would be large and, in theory, ready to repent. Tearing one's garments was the customary sign of grief and alarm. When King Josiah heard the book of the law read, he tore his clothes (2 Kings 22:11). The narrator's remark in verse 24 that no one tore their garments is meant to be heard against that memory: the son does the opposite of the father.
literary: The chapter is built as three readings of the same scroll to three audiences, rising in rank: the people in the temple (verses 9 to 10), the officials in the scribe's chamber (verses 11 to 19), and the king in his winter room (verses 20 to 26). Each reading provokes a different response, from silence, to fear and protective action, to contempt. The narrative moves slowly through names, rooms, and gates, then accelerates as the king cuts and burns. The frame at beginning and end mirrors itself: God commands a scroll, Baruch writes it at dictation, and after the burning God commands another. The repeated word "perhaps" (verses 3 and 7) shows the purpose of the whole exercise. The scroll was written in hope.

outline.t: God commands a scroll of all his words
The scroll read to the people on a fast day
The officials hear it and hide Baruch and Jeremiah
Jehoiakim burns the scroll and orders arrests
A second scroll and a verdict on the king

doctrines.note: The chapter shows the word of God passing from spoken prophecy to written text through a human scribe, and it treats the written scroll as "the words of the LORD" (verse 8). A king can destroy the material but not the message; God simply has it written again.
God's stated aim is not doom but turning: "Then I will forgive their iniquity and their sin" (verse 3). Judgment announced in advance is an invitation, and the warning is itself an act of mercy.
Refusing the word is itself the sin that seals judgment. Jehoiakim's destruction of the scroll brings a sentence on him, his line, and the city (verses 29 to 31).

words.note: Megillah, scroll, a rolled writing. The word appears again and again in this chapter, keeping the physical object in view. Later Jewish tradition used the same word for the five short books read at festivals (such as Esther), but here it simply means the roll Baruch wrote and the king burned.

Shuv, to turn or return, the Old Testament's main word for repentance. It pictures someone walking one way who turns around. Verses 3 and 7 hope that each person "will turn from his wicked way", which is the whole purpose of the scroll.

Salach, to forgive. In the Hebrew Bible this verb always has God as its subject; people pardon, but this word names God's forgiveness. Its presence in verse 3 shows what God was offering through the very scroll the king destroyed.

Saraph, to burn. It is used here of the king burning the scroll (verses 25 to 29), and elsewhere in Jeremiah of the Babylonians burning the city (37:8, 39:8). The echo is deliberate: the king who burned the word will see his city burned.

christ: The chapter tells of a king of David's line who silenced the word of God, and it ends with the promise that Jehoiakim "will have no one to sit on David's throne" (verse 30). The New Testament presents Jesus as the true son of David who does the opposite: he doesn't resist the word but embodies it, the Word made flesh (John 1:14). Jesus himself taught that his words would outlast heaven and earth, which is exactly what this chapter dramatizes: the scroll is burned and returns longer. The link to Christ here is thematic rather than predictive. It shows the pattern of a word that powers try to destroy and that God keeps restoring, a pattern that reaches its height when the world rejected the Word himself, and God raised him.

hard.q: Jeremiah says Jehoiakim will have no one on David's throne and his body will be thrown out, but his son Jehoiachin reigned after him, and 2 Kings 24:6 says he rested with his fathers. Was the prophecy wrong?
hard.a: The difficulty is real. Jehoiachin did succeed his father, but he reigned only three months before Nebuchadnezzar deported him to Babylon in 597 BC (2 Kings 24:8-15), and Jeremiah 22:30 says none of his offspring would sit on the throne. Many interpreters read "no one to sit on David's throne" as meaning no lasting successor, no dynasty that continued through him, which is what happened. On the body, 2 Kings uses the common formula of resting with one's fathers, which usually marks a death without necessarily describing a burial, and it doesn't say where Jehoiakim was buried. Some think his body was disgraced during the Babylonian advance of 598/597 BC; others read Jeremiah's words (here and in 22:19) as a prophetic judgment expressed in the stock language of dishonor. Scripture doesn't record how it was fulfilled, and it is fair to say so.

questions: The officials were afraid when they heard the scroll, but the king was not. What makes some people tremble at a warning while others treat it as an insult?
Jehoiakim didn't argue with the scroll; he destroyed it a few columns at a time. In what quieter ways do people cut away the parts of Scripture they don't want to hear?
God's purpose in writing down judgment was that people might turn and be forgiven. How does that change the way you hear the hard warnings of the Bible?
